author: Matthew Doran
full_text: Houthis declare maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, escalating threat to energy supplies Mon 20 Jul 2026 at 11:02pm , updatedTue 21 Jul 2026 at 10:17am In short: The Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, effective immediately, targeting ships carrying Saudi exports through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis claim they are acting in response to Saudi Arabia's "oppressive siege" on Yemen over the past 12 years. The move could put even greater pressure on international energy supplies. The Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, in a move that could put even greater pressure on international energy supplies. In a statement, the Houthis military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group would enforce the blockade against its "criminal Saudi enemy", effective immediately. He said the Houthis were acting in response to Saudi Arabia's "oppressive siege" on Yemen over the past 12 years, and promised the rebels would respond to "any foolish act" by their neighbour to break the restrictions with force. Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry condemned the statements made by the "so-called military spokesman of the terrorist Houthi militi", adding that Riyadh "continues to support the brotherly Yemeni people and their legitimate government". After the Houthis announced their blockade, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said in a statement that it would respond to them with force, and also that it began implementing protection measures for its ships moving through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The waterway has become a key export route for Saudi oil after the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The internationally-recognised government in Yemen has been blocked from exporting oil by the Houthis, which controls northern Yemen. In a televised address, Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen's Saudi-backed presidential council, said his government had exercised in the past "the highest degrees of restraint" after Houthis targeted vital oil facilities in the country. The war between the US, Israel and Iran sent shock waves through energy markets given the decision by Tehran to block the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world's oil supplies flowed. While smaller gulf states such as Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar suffered major disruption to their exports as a result, Saudi Arabia had been able to use its geography to its advantage and pump oil from its large port precincts on the Persian Gulf to facilities on the west coast. That allowed it to send shipments out through the Red Sea instead — providing a vital lifeline for the Saudi economy and relieving some, but not all, of the pressure on global oil supplies. The east-west pipeline, as it is known, had come under attack by Iran at the height of the war. Blockade expected to target Saudi exports in Bab el-Mandeb Strait The new blockade announced by the Houthis suggested the group would target ships carrying Saudi exports transiting through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — the narrow waterway between Yemen and the Horn of Africa, acting as the gateway to the Red Sea. It is not clear whether it will cause further disruption to shipping in the area, given the Red Sea also feeds into the Suez Canal. The Houthis have previously attacked ships transiting through in protest over the Israel-Gaza war — a move that forced global shipping companies to take massive detours to avoid the area. The Houthis and the Saudis have been in conflict for more than a decade, as civil war ripped Yemen apart and the Saudis formed a coalition to try to restore the Yemeni government's rule. A truce brokered in 2022 had largely held until last week, when the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Yemen's main international airport in a bid to prevent an Iranian plane landing there. The rebels fired missiles in response. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had threatened to use the Houthis to block the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, as fighting between the US and Iran intensified last week.
